note: The source's image (the rock on which the barbarian was wrecked was himself) is dropped and 'errors' is added.
replacement: “You are responsible for all this. It was you who first let them fortify their city after the Median war, and later build the long walls. Then and now you keep depriving of freedom not only the peoples they have enslaved but even your own allies up to now. The true author of a people’s subjugation is not so much the one who carries it out as the power that could prevent it and permits it, above all when that power claims the glory of being the liberator of Hellas. At last we are gathered here, though gathering was not easy, and even now our aims are not settled. We should no longer be asking whether we have been wronged. We should be asking how to defend ourselves. The aggressors have matured plans, and against our indecision they have put aside threats and moved to action. We know the paths along which Athenian aggression travels, and how insidiously it advances. She may take some confidence from thinking that your dullness of perception keeps you from noticing her. But that is nothing beside the impulse she will gain from knowing that you do see, and do not care to interfere. You, Lacedaemonians, alone of all the Hellenes, do nothing. You defend yourselves not by acting but by seeming about to act. You alone wait until an enemy’s power has doubled, when you could have crushed it in its infancy. Yet you had a name for being dependable; in your case, we fear, that name said more than the truth. As we ourselves know, the Mede had time to come from the ends of the earth to Peloponnese, and no force of yours worth mentioning went out to meet him. But he was a distant enemy. Athens at least is a near neighbor, and still you utterly ignore her. Against Athens you choose defense over attack, and you leave the outcome to chance by postponing the struggle until she is far stronger than she was. And you know that, on the whole, the rock on which the barbarian was wrecked was himself, and that if Athens, our present enemy, has not many times destroyed us, we owe that more to her blunders than to your protection. Indeed, hopes placed in you have before now ruined some, whose faith made them neglect to prepare.
